paras: The expulsion of a Black clergyman from Scranton, Kansas, took place one evening in the summer of 1900, when several miners forced an elderly Black minister back onto the train he had just left at the Osage County town. The Topeka State Ledger reported the incident as proof that no Black man was allowed to stop in Scranton, and it called the town a second Gomorrah.

According to the State Ledger, Scranton, in Osage County and about 20 miles from the paper's office, let no "colored man" stop there "on business or otherwise." The paper insisted that "these are facts" and added that few places in the South refused a Black man a stay of a few hours.

"The other evening," an "old colored clergyman" bound for Carbondale got off at Scranton by mistake. He had "scarcely alighted," the item said, when "several big burly miners" rushed up to him and forced him back onto the train. The report gives neither the clergyman's name nor an exact date, and it mentions no injury.
No report of arrests, an official response or any follow-up appears in the coverage.

The incident is known from a single unsigned item on the front page of the State Ledger, a Black weekly in Topeka, on August 11, 1900. Headed "SGDOM AND GOMORAH NO.2," the item called Scranton "this little hell" and "a Gomorah." It ran on a page given mostly to Kansas Republican politics and to the paper's complaints about officials it said ignored or disliked Black voters.
No white newspaper report of the incident was found, and no other Black paper carried it.
